In the
Supreme Court of the United States
____________
LEARNING RESOURCES , ET AL.,
Petitioners,

DONALD J. TRUMP, ET AL.,
     Respondents.

i
QUESTION PRESENTED

 Whether 50 U.S.C. § 170 2(a)(1)(B) grants the
President legal authority to impose tariffs.

1
INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE*

Washington Legal Foundation is a nonprofit,
public-interest law firm and policy center with
supporters nationwide. WLF promotes free markets,
individual rights, limited government, and the rule of
law. It often appears as amicus before this Court in
cases in which one branch of the federal government
has usurped the powers of another, Lucia v. SEC, 585
U.S. 237 (2018) , and has urged th e Court to review
such cases on an expedited basis when that unlawful
action risks significant uncertainty for the American
economy, Nat’l Fed’n of Indep. Bus. v. U.S. Dep’t of
Labor, Occupational Safety & Health Admin. , 595
U.S. 109 (2022) (NFIB).

INTRODUCTION AND
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT

This case should skip the line for two reasons.

First, the President’s legal basis for his
authority to impose tariffs is wrong. “The President’s
power, if any, to issue” such an “order must stem
either from an act of Congress or from the
Constitution itself.” Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v.
Sawyer, 343 U.S. 579, 585 (1952).  While President
Trump claims no Article II tariff power, he does claim
that the International Emergency Economic  Powers

* No party’s counsel authored any part of this brief. No
person or entity, other than Washington Legal Foundation and
its counsel, paid for the brief’ s preparation and submission.
Because the brief is filed more than 10 days before the deadline,
the brief itself serves as notice to all parties.

2
Act (IEEPA) functions as such. But IEEPA does not
involve tariff authorities at all. App. 21a-22a.

The President’s resort to two “vague terms,” W.
Va. v. EPA, 597 U.S. 697, 723  (2022) (internal
quotation marks and citation omitted) , separated
from each other by sixteen words and tucked away in
a 76-word operative subsection, are precisely the sort
of “cryptic,” FDA v. Brown & Williamson Tobacco
Corp., 52 9 U.S. 120, 160 (2000), claim to  vast
executive authority with major economic
consequences that this Court has repeatedly
condemned. Cf. Biden v. Neb. , 600 U.S. 477 (2023) ;
Ala. Ass’n of Realtors v. U.S. Dep’t of H HS, 594 U.S.
758 (2021).

Second, so long as the President claims this
power, businesses throughout the Nation must
assume he will continue to wield it . In prior cases
when the Court has granted the writ before judgment,
tens or hundreds of billions of dollars in activity were
in issue. Biden, 600 U.S. at 502; Ala. Ass’n of Realtors,
594 U.S. at 764 . Here, the President’s actions affect
trillions of dollars’ worth of economic activity , with a
direct impact on the purchasing, production, and
pricing decisions of every American business that
touches, even remotely, international trade.

Businesses “crave certainty as much as almost
anything: certainty is what allows them to make longterm plans and long -term investments.” Alan
Greenspan and Adrian Wooldridge, Capitalism in
America: A History 258 (2018). Already the President
has modified some of these tariffs in response to
outside events. Already one court has extinguished
the tariffs wholesale —only to see that judgment

3
formally stayed. Businesses up and down the supply
chain cannot plan around, or wait for , further
executive modifications, the resolution of stop -andstart injunctions, or circuit percolation. Only this
Court can provide the finality and certainty that
America’s businesses need.

ARGUMENT

I. IEEPA DOES NOT GIVE THE PRESIDENT
LEGAL AUTHORITY TO IMPOSE TARIFFS.

No Article II tariff power exists. The
Constitution gives the tariff power to Congress , and
only Congress can authorize the President to “lay and
collect Taxes, Duties, Imposts, and Excises.” U.S.
Const., art. I, § 8.

So the President must point to clear
authorization in statutory text to unilaterally set
tariff rates. Ala. Ass’n of Realtors, 594 U.S. at 764
(“We expect Congress to speak clearly when
authorizing [the Executive] . . . to exercise powers of
‘vast economic and political significance’”) (quoting
Utility Air Regulatory Grp. v. EPA, 573 U.S. 302, 324
(2014)).

The President points to IEEPA. See, e.g.,
Executive Orders 14298, 14266, 14259, 14257, 14256,
14245, 14232, 14231, 14195, 14194, 14193. He has
done so to impose specific tariffs on some of the
Nation’s largest trading partners. E.g. , Executive
Orders 14193 (Canada), 14194 (Mexico), 14195
(China). He has done so to impose reciprocal rates on
other countries to improve America’s balance -ofpayments. Executive Order 14257 . And he has done

4
so to impose a more-or-less universal floor tariff of ten
percent on all foreign goods sold in the United States.
Id. Some of those tariffs have been altered or held in
abeyance (for now), but not all. What certainly hasn’t
changed i s the President’s claim that IEEPA gives
him a free hand to tariff.

Yet IEEPA does not vest the President with
any power to issue tariffs. “IEEPA does not use the
words ‘tariffs’ or ‘duties,’ their synonyms, or any other
similar terms like ‘customs,’ ‘taxes,’ or ‘imposts.’” App.
21a. This is unsurprising. IEEPA is an economic
sanctions statute with wartime or near -wartime
measures in mind. Pub. Law. 95-223 (enacting IEEPA
“[w]ith respect to the powers of the President in time
of war or national emergency”). President Carter, who
signed IEEPA, deemed it a “largely procedural ”
statute which, if anything,  “place[d] additional
constraints” on “the President’s emergency economic
powers.” Statement of President Carter on Signing
H.R. 7738 Into Law (Dec. 28, 1977) ,
https://perma.cc/3YDP-NW3Z; Sacks v. Off ice of
Foreign Assets Control , 466 F.3d 764, 776 (9th Cir.
2006) (“IEEPA was passed by Congress to counter the
perceived abuse of emergency controls by [P]residents
to unilaterally sanction foreign governments or
interfere with international trade in non -emergency,
peacetime situations”).

Even so, the President —the only Chief
Executive to ever use IEEPA as a tariffing
authority—finds Congressional authorization in this
provision:

[T]he President may,  under such
regulations as he may prescribe, by

5
means of instructions, licenses, or
otherwise . . . investigate, block during
the pendency of an investigation,
regulate, direct and compel, nullify, void,
prevent or prohibit, any acquisition,
holding, withholding, use, transfer,
withdrawal, transportation, importation
or exportation of, or dealing in, or
exercising any right, power, or privilege
with respect to, or transactions
involving, any property in which any
foreign country or a national thereof has
any interest by any person, or with
respect to any property, sub ject to the
jurisdiction of the United States[.]

50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B) (emphasis supplied).

The district court correctly rejected this open -
ended reading, which conflates the power to regulate
with the power to tax. App. 23a (“To regulate is to
establish rules governing conduct; to tariff is to raise
revenue through taxes on imports or exports”).
Neither the investigative powers discussed before the
word “regulate,” nor the sixteen words between
“regulate” and “importation,” raise even the ghost of
a tariff authority. Far from rote rate -setting of
customs duties, those sixteen words  involve
compellence, voidance, prevention —traditional
national-security or wartime aims one would expect
in a sanctions authority.

After all, Congress has already enumerated the
circumstances under which the President may impose
tariffs—as opposed to sanctions or an embargo —for
national security reasons. 19 U.S.C. § 1862 (requiring

6
time-delimited investigation and report by the
Commerce Secretary before the President may
impose new tariffs for “[s]afeguarding national
security”). IEEPA’s “largely procedural” text neither
adds to nor subtract s from that grant of authority.
Statement of President Carter on Signing H.R. 7738
Into Law (Dec. 28, 1977).

In sum, t he President rests his legal
justification on two plucked words, sixteen apart (out
of 76 operative words in the relevant subsection), with
one of those plucked words given an uncommon
meaning. App. 22a (“‘Tariff’ and ‘regulate’ also take
different plain meanings”). “Extraordinary grants of
regulatory authority,” such as a unilateral
Presidential writ to impose tariffs, “are rarely
accomplished through ‘ modest words,’ ‘vague terms,’
or ‘subtle device[s].’” W. Va., 597 U.S. at 723 (quoting
Whitman v. Am. Trucking Ass’ns, 531 U.S. 457, 468
(2001)) (brackets in original) ; cf. Utility Air
Regulatory Grp., 573 U.S. at  324 (“When an agency
claims to discover in a long -extant statute an
unheralded power to regulate ‘a significant portion of
the American economy ’” courts must “typically greet
its announcement with a measure of skepticism”)
(quoting Brown & Williamson, 529 U.S. at 159).

The President’s reliance on “regulate . . .
importation” sings in the same key  as past
unconstitutional Executive Branch practice that
purported to  find remarkable Congressional
delegations of authority in a pocket of the U.S. Code.
“Regulate” no more grants the Executive a tariff
power than “waive or modify” granted a power to
cancel debt, Bide n, 600 U.S. at 506, “necessary”
granted a power to freeze evictions nationwide, Ala.

7
Ass’n of Realtors, 594 U.S. at 765, or “drug” gave carte
blanche to regulate tobacco  products. Brown &
Williamson, 529 U.S. at 125.

In short, IEEPA delegate s no general tariff
power to the Executive. Such “a sweeping and
consequential authority” would not have been
granted to the Executive “‘in so cryptic a fashion’” as
the President’s strained reading of the statute
suggests. W. Va., 597 U.S. at 721 (quoting Brown &
Williamson, 529 U.S. at 160).

And the stakes are too high for this Court not
to say so now.

II. ONLY THIS COURT CAN PROVIDE
CERTAINTY AND FINALITY ON THAT
QUESTION.

Whether here or in another case, this Court
must reckon with the Question Presented . See ECF
No. 53, V.O.S. Selections, Inc. v. Trump, Case No. 25-
1812 (Fed. Cir. June 1 3, 2025) (setting accelerated
briefing schedule). There’s no reason to wait. As in
other separation-of-powers cases in which the Court
has expedited review, this is a straightforward
statutory interpretation case with “staggering”
economic consequences. Biden, 600 U.S. at 502; id. at
489 (noting grant of certiorari before judgment);
NFIB, 595 U.S. at 113 (emergency application for stay
granted).

It is an understatement to call the Question
Presented a trillion-dollar question. In 2024, the sum
of the Nation ’s international trade in goods and
services was over seven trillion dollars. Bureau of

8
Economic Analysis, “ U.S. International Trade in
Goods and Services, December and Annual 2024, ”
U.S. Dep ’t of Commerce (Feb . 5, 2025) ;
https://perma.cc/9XJT-237N. Whether IEEPA vests
the President with a unilateral tariff authority is a
question with purchasing, production, and pricing
decisions for every business in America that engages,
even in an ancillary fashion, in the international
marketplace.

If IEEPA is (properly) set to the side, the
Executive is largely capable of imposing tariffs only
via authorities that are either strictly time-limited, 19
U.S.C. § 2132(a), require a pre-tariff investigation, or
have a notice period before rates go into effect. App.
25a (discussing relevant statutes ). Time limits
provide market actors with a date certain for
executive-only tariffs to expire. Time lags provide
market actors with lead time to adjust (or petition for
change).

But if IEEPA is  a freestanding grant to the
President, rates can immediately change from day to
day under the Executive’s policy preferences. Indeed,
President Trump has repeatedly adjusted his IEEPA-
authority tariff rates in response to business feedback
and negotiations with foreign nations. E.g., Executive
Orders 14298, 14259.

Figuring out how to, say, fill shelves with
enough inventory  by Christmas in such
circumstances is a heavy lift.  Scott Lincicome, “Toys,
Pencils, and Poverty at the Margins,” Cato Inst., May
7, 2025, https://perma.cc/9Z2Y-UBP2 (observing that
“97 percent of toys purchased in the United States are
imported”). Tariffs are taxes, and “frequent tax

9
changes are the greatest factor in business
uncertainty affecting investment and growth.” Xuan-
Thao Nguyen and Jeffrey A. Maine, Attacking
Innovation, 99 B.U. L. Rev. 1687, 1738 (2019).

If the business community must live with the
uncertainty of a moving target, it at least ought to be
certain how the target can move. And if the IEEPA
tariffs are unlawful, then this business uncertainty is
being imposed on “a significant portion of the
American economy” for naught. Utility Air Regulatory
Grp., 573 U.S. at 324  (internal quotation marks and
citation omitted). Either way, there’s no reason to let
this drag on.

Leaving percolation to the lower courts risks
causing more harm.  There have already been
moments where a single court extinguished the
President’s tariffs wholesale, V.O.S. Selections, Inc. v.
Trump, Case No. 25 -66 (Ct. of Int’l Trade May 28,
2025), only for another to turn them back on. ECF No.
51, V.O.S. Selections, Inc. v. Trump, Case No. 25-1812
(Fed. Cir. June 10, 2025) (order granting stay).
Businesses throughout the supply chain should not
have to contend with f urther whipsawing from stopand-start injunctions, or plan around the possibility
of a circuit division developing on this multi-trilliondollar question.

As the sole  judicial body with nationwide
authority and finality-of-opinion, U.S. Const. art. III,
only this Court can resolve this uncertainty for
America’s businesses and consumers.

10

CONCLUSION

The Court should grant the writ ahead of
judgment.

      Respectfully submitted,

Cory L. Andrews
Zac Morgan
   Counsel of Record
WASHINGTON LEGAL FOUNDATION
